transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. Well, I'm here because... I just don't feel much of anything good lately. It's like... even when my children come over to sit with me, or when the sun is shining right on my garden—things that usually make me smile—I just feel completely flat inside. It's as if the part of me that could feel glad or comforted just... shut off entirely.
How long have you been feeling this way—unable to feel pleasure or joy even in things you used to enjoy?

It's been... well, about two weeks now. It started right after my husband collapsed. The paramedics came and were working on him right there in our kitchen, and... ever since that day, I've just felt this way.
What happened to your husband after that day—is he still alive, or did he pass away?

I... I'm really not sure. They put him in the ambulance and took him to the hospital that day. But since then, I just haven't been able to get a clear answer from anyone about what's happening. I just know he isn't at home.
Have you tried calling the hospital or asking your children directly about your husband's condition, and if so, what happened when you tried?

I... well, I haven't tried calling the hospital. I suppose I could, but... I just haven't. And my children, they come over and sit with me, but I haven't asked them either. I don't know why, really. I just haven't been able to bring myself to ask.
Since your husband collapsed, have you noticed any changes in your sleep or appetite—like sleeping much more or less than usual, or having little interest in eating?

I haven't really noticed any big changes with my sleep or my eating. I suppose things are mostly the same as they were before... I'm still eating my meals and sleeping about the same amount. I just... I don't think anything has really changed there.

Since your husband collapsed, have you had any moments where you suddenly relive that scene in your mind, or feel like you're detached from what's happening around you, as if you're in a daze or not quite real?

Well, I do have moments where things don't feel quite real. Sometimes I'll just be walking through my own kitchen, and... it looks like a room in someone else's house. It's a very strange feeling. I just feel like I'm moving around in a dream, and like I'm not really there at all.

Do you find yourself avoiding certain places, activities, or conversations—like standing in the kitchen where it happened, or talking about your husband's condition—because they remind you of that day?

No, I don't think I'm avoiding anything like that. I still go into the kitchen just fine... I mean, I have to, to make my meals and get my tea. And, well, I know I mentioned I haven't asked the kids about his condition, but it's not really because it reminds me of that day. I just haven't done it. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm staying away from any rooms or conversations on purpose.
Besides feeling emotionally flat, have you noticed feeling unusually tired or low on energy, having trouble concentrating, or feeling worthless or guilty since your husband collapsed?

Well, I wouldn't say I feel worthless or guilty, and my energy is mostly okay. But... I have noticed that I'm having a lot of trouble concentrating. I used to plan all my meals and keep my calendar straight without any problem. Now, I just stare at a grocery list or the schedule for the senior center, and my mind goes completely blank. I can't seem to figure it out. My daughter has had to step in and help me decide on even the simplest things, because I just can't seem to focus enough to do it myself.
Since your husband collapsed, have you noticed feeling unusually jumpy or on edge, like you startle easily or your heart races even when nothing is happening?

Yes, I have been very jumpy. It doesn't even take much. If the refrigerator just clicks on, or if someone knocks at the front door, I jump so hard my whole body shakes. It really startles me, and then it takes a long while before my heart settles down and stops racing.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient developed a cluster of symptoms within days after witnessing a severe, life-threatening traumatic event (her husband's collapse and resuscitation). Symptoms have persisted for about 2 weeks (within the 3-day-to-1-month window defining an acute stress reaction) and include marked emotional numbing/inability to experience positive emotion, dissociative symptoms (derealization—feeling her own kitchen looks unfamiliar, feeling as if in a dream), impaired concentration, and pronounced hyperarousal (exaggerated startle response, racing heart). There is no avoidance behavior, and vegetative symptoms (sleep, appetite) are unaffected, arguing against a major depressive episode. The symptom duration is too short and too temporally tied to a single identifiable stressor to meet PTSD criteria (which requires symptoms beyond 1 month), making Acute Stress Disorder (F43.0) the most fitting diagnosis. PTSD (F43.10) remains a differential if symptoms persist beyond one month, and Major Depressive Disorder (F32.9) was considered but is less consistent given intact sleep/appetite and clear precipitating trauma with dissociative/hyperarousal features.
